questions.html: Which of the following options is/are true?

options.html: If only the last two operations out of many in a committed transaction do not take effect, it is a violation of the Atomicity principle.
Interleaving transactions is always faster than doing them one at a time.
Transaction A reads from relation W, and Transaction B reads from relation W concurrently. They may possibly read any or all of W. This is considered a conflict.
Transaction A writes to relation W, and Transaction B writes to relation W concurrently. They may possibly write to any or all of W. This is considered a conflict.

questions.solution:
Answer: Not available

Source solution 1 (score: 0)

$A$ is a violation of the Atomicity principle.

$B$, there could be no conflicts and since interleaving has a significant overhead cost, interleaving could actually run slower.

$C$ is false because a conflict requires at least one operation to be a write and both operations here are reads.

$D$ is a definition of a conflict

questions.html:
The following two transactions are run concurrently:

$T_{1}: r_{1}(A) ; w_{1}(B) ; c_{1}$

$T_{2}: w_{2}(A) ; r_{2}(B) ; c_{2}$

Depending on the scheduler, we may get various combinations of the actions of $T_{1}$ and $T_{2}$. One example of a resulting schedule could be

$S: r_{1}(A) ; w_{1}(B) ; w_{2}(A) ; r_{2}(B) ; c_{1} ; c_{2}$

How many interleavings of these two transactions are there?
questions.solution:
Answer: Not available

Source solution 1 (score: 1)

The total number of operations from both transactions combined is 6, since transaction $T_1$ has 3 operations and transaction $T_2$ has 3 operations.

The total number of distinct ways to arrange or interleave these 6 operations while strictly maintaining the internal order of each individual transaction is given by the formula $\frac{6!}{3! \times 3!}$.

Calculating this value gives $\frac{720}{6 \times 6} = \frac{720}{36} = 20$.

In standard database terminology and within the context of this specific problem, the term "interleavings" refers to the total set of all valid concurrent and serial schedules combined.

Therefore, the exact number of allowed interleavings for these two transactions is 20.

Source solution 2 (score: 0)

Place the transactions of T1 in one order( there is only one order in which we can place them)

Now there are 4 places(2 in between and 2 on the sides) where we can place the actions of T2

 

First Case-> No actions are together, for example w2(A);r2(B) don't occur one after the other
In this case every action of T2 is alone, so we need to select 3 slots out of 4 which gives us
4C3=4 ways
For example, One way to arrange is
r1​(A);w2(A);w1​(B);r2(B);c1;c2;


Second Case-> Two actions of T2 occur one after the other, so two actions require only 1 slot,
So, we need to select 2 slots out of 4 which gives us 4C2=6 ways

For the chosen pair of slots, there are 2 ways to distribute the actions while preserving order:

first slot gets 2 actions, second gets 1

first slot gets 1 action, second gets 2

So for the second case number of ways =6*2=12 ways

Third Case -> All actions of Transaction T2 occur together as one entity
This gives us 4C1=4 ways

Adding all the Cases we get 4+12+4= 20 ways to arrange

questions.html:
Consider the following two transactions:

$T_{1}: r_{1}(A) ; w_{1}(A) ; r_{1}(B) ; w_{1}(B)$;

$T_{2}: r_{2}(B) ; w_{2}(B) ; r_{2}(A) ; w_{2}(A)$;

Among the possible schedules of the eight actions above, how many are conflict-equivalent to the serial order ($T_1,T_2$)?
questions.solution:
Answer: Not available

Source solution 1 (score: 0)

Questions says:

how many are conflict-equivalent to the serial order (T1,T2)

This means the serial order $(T_1, T_2)$ is our reference point. We are strictly looking for schedules that match the conflict behavior of $T_1$ running first and $T_2$ running second.

On the data item $B$, a Write-Read conflict exists between $w_1(B)$ and $r_2(B)$, which strictly forces the constraint $w_1(B) \rightarrow r_2(B)$.

From the internal program order of the individual transactions, $w_1(B)$ is the absolute last operation of $T_1$, while $r_2(B)$ is the absolute first operation of $T_2$.

Combining these , all operations of $T_1$ must completely execute before any operation of $T_2$ can begin.

Because the last operation of $T_1$ must finish before the first operation of $T_2$ can even begin, the entire schedule collapses into a single rigid chain:

$$\underbrace{r_1(A) \longrightarrow w_1(A) \longrightarrow r_1(B) \longrightarrow w_1(B)}_{\text{All of } T_1} \;\mathbf{\bf\longrightarrow}\; \underbrace{r_2(B) \longrightarrow w_2(B) \longrightarrow r_2(A) \longrightarrow w_2(A)}_{\text{All of } T_2}$$

if we pull an operation from $T_2$ earlier or push an operation from $T_1$ later breakss this chain.

Therefore, the number of conflict-equivalent schedules is exactly 1.

questions.html: This ACID property is something that an application builder has to be at least partly concerned with when writing their application code in order for the other ACID properties to ensure correctness despite other things that might go wrong when running in a multi-user and potentially failure-prone environment.
questions.solution:
Answer: Not available

Source solution 1 (score: 0)

While the DBMS handles Atomicity, Isolation, and Durability natively, the developer must explicitly code the correct business logic to ensure data transitions between valid states.

If a programmer writes faulty code that updates accounts incorrectly (e.g., deducting money from one account without adding it to another), the DBMS will still ensure that the bad data is completely written ($A$), isolated from others ($I$), and saved permanently ($D$). The system cannot automatically know if the programmatic rules make sense.

so option B (Consistency)

questions.html: Suppose that $5$ concurrent transactions are concurrently attempting to read the same record in a table holding bank account information. How many of these transactions will be able to read the record at one time under $2$ PL?
questions.solution:
Answer: Not available

Source solution 1 (score: 0)

Under Two-Phase Locking (2PL), reading a record requires acquiring a Shared Lock (S-lock), and since shared locks are completely compatible with each other, all 5 concurrent transactions can hold the lock and read the record simultaneously.

questions.html:
Consider the following schedule $S$ of transactions $T_1$ and $T_2:$

$${\begin{array}{l|l}
\textbf{T1}&    \textbf{T2} \\\hline
\text{Read(A)} \\
\text{A = A – 10}\\
&   \text{Read(A) }\\  
&  \text{Temp = A} \\
& \text{Write(A)} \\
& \text{Read(B)} \\    
\text{Write(A)}\\
 \text{Read(B)}\\
\text{B = B + 10}\\
\text{Write(B)} \\
& \text{B = B + Temp}  \\  
& \text{Write(B)}\\ 
\end{array}}$$

Which of the following is TRUE about the schedule $S$ ?

options.html: $S$ is serializable both as $T_1, T_2$ and $T_2, T_1$
$S$ is neither serializable as $T_1,T_2$ nor as $T_2,T_1$

questions.solution:
Answer: A

Source solution 1 (score: 0)

Answer: $\text{A}$

$\color{red}{\text{Misconception}} :$ View serializability is necessary and sufficient for serializability.

Given schedule is serializable even though it is neither view serializable nor conflict serializable.

Majority of aspirants has misconception that serializability is same as view serializability. They think view serializability is necessary and sufficient for serializability. But it is not so.

Since computations are also given along with read and write operations, just checking view serializability is not enough to conclude that given schedule is not serializable. Because every view serializable schedule is serializable but not every serializable schedule is view serializable.

From NPTEL:

General Serializability definition from Ullman:

Now, coming to the given question.
We have to check if the effect (final database state) of given schedule in question is same as effect of SOME serial schedule (where transactions execute one after another without interleaving)..

Assume that initially $A=x$ and $B=y$.

Effect of given schedule :

$$ \begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|} \hline \text{T1} & \text{T2} & \text{\color{blue}{A=x}} & \text{\color{blue}{B=y}} \\ \hline \text{Read(A)} & & & \\ \text{A=A-10} & & & \\ & \text{Read(A)} & & \\ & \text{Temp=A} & & \\ & \text{Write(A)} & \text{\color{blue}{A=x}} & \\ & \text{Read(B)} & & \\ \text{Write(A)} & & \text{\color{blue}{A=x-10}} & \\ \text{Read(B)} & & & \\ \text{B=B+10} & & & \\ \text{Write(B)} & & & \text{\color{blue}{B=y+10}} \\ & \text{B=B+\text{Temp}} & & \\ & \text{Write(B)} & & \text{\color{blue}{B=x+y}} \\ \hline & & \text{\color{red}{A=x-10}} & \text{\color{red}{B=x+y}} \\ \hline \end{array} $$

Effect of serial schedule $S_{1} : (T1,T2)$ :

$$ \begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|} \hline \text{T1} & \text{T2} & \text{\color{blue}{A=x}} & \text{\color{blue}{B=y}} \\ \hline \text{Read(A)} & & & \\ \text{A=A-10} & & & \\ \text{Write(A)} & & \text{\color{blue}{A=x-10}} & \\ \text{Read(B)} & & & \\ \text{B=B+10} & & & \\ \text{Write(B)} & & & \text{\color{blue}{B=y+10}} \\ & & & \\[1ex] & \text{Read(A)} & & \\ & \text{Temp=A} & & \\ & \text{Write(A)} & \text{\color{blue}{A=x-10}} & \\ & \text{Read(B)} & & \\ & \text{B=B+\text{Temp}} & & \\ & \text{Write(B)} & & \text{\color{blue}{B=(y+10)+(x-10)}} \\ \hline & & \text{\color{red}{A=x-10}} & \text{\color{red}{B=x+y}} \\ \hline \end{array} $$

Effect of serial schedule $S_{2} : (T2, T1)$ :

$$ \begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|} \hline \text{T1} & \text{T2} & \text{\color{blue}{A=x}} & \text{\color{blue}{B=y}} \\ \hline & \text{Read(A)} & & \\ & \text{Temp=A} & & \\ & \text{Write(A)} & \text{\color{blue}{A=x}} & \\ & \text{Read(B)} & & \\ & \text{B=B+\text{Temp}} & & \\ & \text{Write(B)} & & \text{\color{blue}{B=x+y}} \\ & & & \\[1ex] \text{Read(A)} & & & \\ \text{A=A-10} & & & \\ \text{Write(A)} & & \text{\color{blue}{A=x-10}} & \\ \text{Read(B)} & & & \\ \text{B=B+10} & & & \\ \text{Write(B)} & & & \text{\color{blue}{B=x+y+10}} \\ \hline & & \text{\color{red}{A=x-10}} & \text{\color{red}{B=x+y+10}} \\ \hline \end{array} $$

We can see that for every initial database state, effect of $S_t$ is equal to effect of serial schedule $S_{t1} : (T1, T2)$.

So, given schedule is serializable only as $T1,T2$. Option A is correct, not option D.

Note: 

  • When computations are given in the Schedule, we have to check for general serializability.
  • When computations are not given and only Read and Write operations are given then in that case, Serializability $\equiv$ View Serializability.
  • When computations and blind writes are not there, Serializability $\equiv$ View Serializability $\equiv$ Conflict Serializability.

Under the SERIALIZABLE isolation level, concurrent transactions must yield results equivalent to executing in a purely sequential order ($T_2 \rightarrow T_1$ or $T_1 \rightarrow T_2$).

questions.html: Which of the following options is/are false?

options.html: Depending on what they are doing, it is possible for concurrent transactions to become involved in a deadlock under strict two-phase locking. If this happens, it can lead to an inconsistent database state.
If we know all records that each transaction will access, we can prevent deadlocks by imposing a total order on lock acquisitions.

questions.solution:
Answer: A, B

Source solution 1 (score: 0)

Answer: A, B and C

The key is to evaluate each statement independently.

A. False

Concurrent transactions can become involved in a deadlock under Strict 2PL. If this happens, it can lead to an inconsistent database state.

The first part is true: Strict 2PL can cause deadlock.

For example:

 
T1: Lock-X(A)
T2: Lock-X(B)

T1: Request Lock-X(B) → waits for T2
T2: Request Lock-X(A) → waits for T1

This creates a cycle in the wait-for graph:

T1→T2→T1

Hence, a deadlock occurs.

However, deadlock does not imply an inconsistent database state. Strict 2PL guarantees conflict serializability and recoverability. When a deadlock is detected, one of the transactions can be aborted and rolled back, preserving database consistency.

Therefore, the statement as a whole is false.

A=False​

B. False

Wound-wait always outperforms wait-die.

This is false because there is no universal performance dominance between wound-wait and wait-die.

Recall:

  • Wait-die: Older transaction waits; younger transaction aborts.
  • Wound-wait: Older transaction aborts the younger transaction; younger transaction waits.

Consider:

 
T1 = older
T2 = younger

T2 holds lock on X
T1 requests X

Wait-die:

Since T1 is older:

T1→Wait

If T2 is going to finish soon, T1 waits for a short time and no transaction needs to be aborted.

Wound-wait:

Since T1 is older and X is held by younger T2:

T1→abort T2

If T2 had already performed significant work, that work is lost.

Thus, there are situations where wait-die can perform better than wound-wait.

Hence, wound-wait does not always outperform wait-die.

B=False​

C. False

Wait-die always outperforms wound-wait.

Again, the word "always" makes the statement false.

Consider the same situation:

 
T1 = older
T2 = younger

T2 holds X
T1 requests X

Suppose T2 is a long-running transaction and will hold X for a long time.

Wait-die:

T1 is older, so:

T1→Wait

T1 may have to wait for a long time.

Wound-wait:

T1 is older and X is held by younger T2, so:

T1→abort T2

T1 can then acquire X and continue without waiting for T2.

Thus, in this situation, wound-wait can perform better than wait-die.

Therefore, wait-die does not always outperform wound-wait.

C=False​

D. True

If we know all records that each transaction will access, we can prevent deadlocks by imposing a total order on lock acquisitions.

Suppose we impose:

A<B<C

and require every transaction to acquire locks only according to this order.

For example:

 
Lock(A) → Lock(B) → Lock(C)

is allowed, but:

 
Lock(B) → Lock(A)

is not allowed.

A deadlock requires a cycle in the wait-for graph.

For example:

 
T1 holds A → requests B
T2 holds B → requests A

gives:

T1→T2→T1

which is a deadlock.

But with a global ordering A<B, T2 cannot acquire B first and then request A. Therefore, such a cycle cannot be formed.

Hence, imposing a total ordering on lock acquisition prevents deadlock.

D=True​

Final Answer

A, B, C are FALSE​
